questions.stem:
A 38-year-old healthy woman comes to clinic 8 days before a trip to rural Guatemala, where she will eat in local homes. She has received all routine childhood vaccines but has never had hepatitis A vaccine. She asks whether it is too late for protection against this fecal-oral infection.

Which plan is most appropriate?
choices: Vaccine now plus immune globulin, then a second dose at 6 to 12 months
Skip the vaccine, since it cannot work in under 2 weeks
Give immune globulin alone and defer the vaccine until she returns home
Give the vaccine now and repeat it every 2 years while traveling
Give the live oral vaccine on days 1, 3, 5 and 7 before she departs the country

explain.html:
Hepatitis A and typhoid are the two vaccines to consider for all destinations, because both spread by the fecal-oral route. The hepatitis A vaccine should be given more than two weeks before travel, which is one reason the pretravel visit belongs at least a month before departure. When departure is two weeks or less away, the plan is to give the vaccine and add immune globulin, which covers the traveler while the vaccine response develops. A second dose at 6 to 12 months completes the series and gives lifelong immunity, so repeated boosters are not needed.

This woman leaves in 8 days for rural Guatemala and has never had the vaccine, so it is not too late: she gets the vaccine now with immune globulin, then the second dose 6 to 12 months later. The live oral schedule on days 1, 3, 5 and 7 and the 2-year booster both belong to the typhoid vaccines, not hepatitis A.
why: The vaccine is not skipped when travel is close; immune globulin is added so she is still protected.
Giving immune globulin alone and deferring the vaccine wastes the chance to start the series that gives lifelong immunity.
Two doses of hepatitis A vaccine give lifelong immunity; boosting every 2 years describes the inactivated typhoid vaccine.
The live oral four-dose schedule is the typhoid vaccine, not hepatitis A.
explain.takeaway: Hepatitis A vaccine is given more than 2 weeks before travel; if departure is 2 weeks or less away, immune globulin is added, and a second dose at 6 to 12 months gives lifelong immunity.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 26-year-old man completed the live oral typhoid vaccine (four capsules over a week) before a 3-month trip through South Asia. He tells his travel clinician he plans to eat street food freely and skip water precautions because he is now vaccinated against typhoid.

Which counseling point is most accurate?
choices: The vaccine protects for life, so food precautions are unnecessary
The live vaccine must be followed by the injectable vaccine to work
The vaccine also prevents enterotoxigenic E. coli, so diarrhea risk is low
It is only partly protective, so food and water care is still needed
Freezing ice and adding alcohol to drinks will cover any remaining risk

explain.html:
Typhoid fever is caused by Salmonella Typhi and, like hepatitis A, spreads by the fecal-oral route, so its vaccine is considered for all destinations. There are two vaccines: a live oral vaccine taken on days 1, 3, 5 and 7 and finished at least 1 week before travel, boosted at 5 years, and an inactivated parenteral vaccine given at least 2 weeks before travel, boosted at 2 years. Both are only 50 to 80% protective, so vaccinated travelers still need to be careful with food and water. The vaccine also does nothing for travelers' diarrhea, whose most common cause is enterotoxigenic E. coli.

This man finished the oral vaccine but plans to eat street food freely and drop water precautions, which leaves him exposed to the typhoid the vaccine misses and to every other cause of travelers' diarrhea. Prevention still means hand washing, water purification and careful food choices, remembering that freezing does not kill these organisms and alcohol does not sterilize water or ice: "Boil it, cook it, peel it, or forget it."

VaccineTiming before travelBooster or completionProtection
Hepatitis AMore than 2 weeks (2 weeks or less: add immune globulin)Second dose at 6 to 12 monthsLifelong
Typhoid, live oralDays 1, 3, 5, 7, done at least 1 week beforeBoost at 5 years50 to 80%
Typhoid, inactivated parenteralAt least 2 weeks beforeBoost at 2 years50 to 80%
why: Typhoid vaccines need boosters (5 years oral, 2 years injectable) and are only 50 to 80% protective, so they neither last for life nor remove the need for precautions.
The live oral and inactivated injectable typhoid vaccines are alternatives, not a required sequence.
Typhoid vaccine does not protect against ETEC or any other cause of travelers' diarrhea.
Freezing does not kill the organisms that cause travelers' diarrhea, and alcohol does not sterilize water or ice.
explain.takeaway: Typhoid vaccines (live oral or inactivated injectable) are only 50 to 80% protective and need boosters, so vaccinated travelers still need food and water precautions.

questions.stem:
A 45-year-old man is planning a pilgrimage to Mecca for the Hajj. He also plans to visit relatives in Niger in February. He received routine vaccines as a child, but none in the past 10 years. The infection of concern spreads through respiratory secretions in crowded close contact and peaks across a band of sub-Saharan Africa during the dry season.

Which vaccine is required for the first part of his trip?
choices: Meningococcal conjugate vaccine (ACWY)
Yellow fever live-attenuated vaccine
Serogroup B meningococcal vaccine
Japanese encephalitis vaccine
Inactivated injectable typhoid vaccine given intramuscularly

explain.html:
Meningococcal disease occurs worldwide but has its highest incidence in the meningitis belt of sub-Saharan Africa, and it spreads through respiratory secretions in close contact. Travel protection uses the quadrivalent conjugate vaccine (ACWY). Serogroup B is not considered a travel-related risk, so the B vaccine is not part of travel planning. ACWY is recommended for travel to the meningitis belt, particularly during the dry season (December to June), and it is required for entry to Saudi Arabia during the Hajj, with a booster after 5 years.

This man's Hajj pilgrimage makes the ACWY vaccine an entry requirement for the first part of his trip, and his February visit to Niger falls in the meningitis belt during the dry season, so the same vaccine covers both legs. Yellow fever, Japanese encephalitis and typhoid vaccines are each given for certain destinations or considered for all, but none is the Hajj requirement.
explain.table:
CategoryVaccines
RoutineRoutine vaccinations
Consider for all destinationsHepatitis A, typhoid
Certain destinations or activitiesYellow fever, meningococcal, Japanese encephalitis, rabies, polio, cholera, tick-borne encephalitis, chikungunya
why: Yellow fever vaccine is given for certain destinations where the virus circulates, not as the entry requirement for the Hajj.
Serogroup B is not a travel-related risk, so the B vaccine is not what the Hajj requires.
Japanese encephalitis vaccine is given for certain destinations and activities, not as the Hajj requirement.
Typhoid vaccine is considered for all destinations but is not the vaccine required for Hajj entry.
explain.takeaway: The quadrivalent conjugate meningococcal vaccine (ACWY) is required for entry to Saudi Arabia during the Hajj and recommended for the sub-Saharan meningitis belt in the dry season, with a booster after 5 years.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 24-year-old woman develops watery, non-bloody diarrhea with cramps on day 6 of a stay at an all-inclusive resort in Mexico. She has 4 to 5 loose stools a day, no fever and is still able to enjoy most activities. Symptoms resolve after 3 days with oral fluids.

Which organism most likely caused her illness?
choices: Shigella species
Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli
Giardia lamblia
Enteroaggregative Escherichia coli (EAEC)
Campylobacter jejuni

explain.html:
Travelers' diarrhea is the most common illness in travelers to developing countries, affecting 40 to 60% of them. Most cases begin 4 to 14 days after arrival and are self-limited over 1 to 5 days, and chemoprophylaxis is generally not recommended. Risk is high in South and Southeast Asia, Africa outside South Africa, South and Central America, and Mexico; it is highest in the first week and with street vendor food, all-inclusive lodging and visiting family or friends. Bacteria cause more than 90% of cases, and enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC), called "turista," is the most common offender, followed by enteroaggregative E. coli, Salmonella, Shigella, C. jejuni and others, with viruses and parasites causing the rest.

This woman's watery, nonbloody diarrhea without fever on day 6 at a Mexican all-inclusive resort, mild enough that she kept up her activities and gone in 3 days, is the typical picture. The best single answer for its cause is ETEC, because it is the most common organism behind exactly this pattern.
why: Shigella is a listed cause, but it typically produces dysentery with fever and blood and is far less common than ETEC.
Giardia is one of the less common parasitic causes, and this short watery illness fits the dominant bacterial cause.
EAEC is a listed bacterial cause, but ETEC is named the most common offender.
Campylobacter is a listed bacterial cause but far less common than ETEC.
explain.takeaway: Travelers' diarrhea begins 4 to 14 days after arrival, is self-limited, is caused by bacteria in more than 90% of cases, and is most often due to enterotoxigenic E. coli.
explain.subject: Microbiology

rows.why: Shigella is a listed cause, but it typically produces dysentery with fever and blood and is far less common than ETEC.

rows.if_right: stool testing that found Giardia, a parasitic cause behind a small share of cases

questions.stem:
A 35-year-old journalist leaves tomorrow for a 10-day assignment in a region of West Africa with chloroquine-resistant Plasmodium falciparum. He wants the prophylaxis option that can start right away and that he can stop soonest after he gets home, because he dislikes taking pills for weeks.

Which regimen best fits his needs?
choices: Chloroquine weekly, starting 1 to 2 weeks before travel
Mefloquine weekly, starting 2 to 3 weeks before and continued 4 weeks after
Atovaquone-proguanil daily, from 1 day before until 7 days after
Doxycycline daily, starting 1 to 2 days before and continued 4 weeks after
No pills, using only DEET and bed nets to prevent mosquito bites

explain.html:
Malaria is caused by intraerythrocytic Plasmodium protozoa spread by mosquitoes, and chemoprophylaxis must start before travel, continue during exposure and continue after leaving the endemic area. The regimens differ in where they can be used and in how long they run before and after. Chloroquine is only for chloroquine-susceptible areas and starts 1 to 2 weeks before; mefloquine starts 2 to 3 weeks before; both continue 4 weeks after. Doxycycline starts 1 to 2 days before but also continues 4 weeks after the last exposure. Atovaquone-proguanil starts 1 day before and continues only 7 days after.

This journalist leaves tomorrow for a chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum area and wants the shortest course after he returns, so atovaquone-proguanil fits. Mosquito bite prevention, including DEET, treated bed nets, screened rooms and avoiding the outdoors from dusk to dawn, adds to chemoprophylaxis but does not replace it.
explain.table:
DrugStart before travelContinue after last exposureNote
Chloroquine1 to 2 weeks4 weeksOnly chloroquine-susceptible areas
Mefloquine2 to 3 weeks4 weeksWeekly
Doxycycline1 to 2 days4 weeksDaily, least expensive
Atovaquone-proguanil1 day7 daysDaily
TafenoquineDaily loading dose for 3 days7 daysWeekly after loading
why: Chloroquine is only for chloroquine-susceptible areas, and it must start 1 to 2 weeks before travel.
Mefloquine must start 2 to 3 weeks before travel and continues 4 weeks after, so it fails both of his needs.
Doxycycline can start 1 to 2 days before travel but continues 4 weeks after the last exposure, the long tail he wants to avoid.
Bite prevention alone is not enough for exposure to falciparum malaria; it adds to chemoprophylaxis.
explain.takeaway: Malaria chemoprophylaxis continues after exposure: atovaquone-proguanil runs from 1 day before to 7 days after, while chloroquine, mefloquine and doxycycline continue 4 weeks after the last exposure.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 29-year-old man returns from Ghana 10 days ago with fever, chills and headache. He did not take prophylaxis. A STAT blood smear shows ring forms inside red cells. He is drowsy and responds only to loud voice.

[[labs 0]]

Which statement best describes his illness?
choices: Uncomplicated malaria, because his blood pressure is normal
Uncomplicated malaria, because only falciparum causes severe disease
Severe malaria, from parasitemia of 5% or more and altered mentation
Severe malaria only if a repeat smear in 48 hours shows a rising parasite count
Dengue with a false-positive smear, because both cause fever and anemia

explain.html:
The rule for a febrile traveler from a malarious area is that fever is malaria until proven otherwise, so the workup is a history and physical, a STAT malaria smear and prompt therapy. Uncomplicated malaria can occur with any Plasmodium species and means parasitemia under 5%, a patient who is not obtunded, can take oral medicines and has no vital organ dysfunction. Severe or complicated malaria is usually P. falciparum and is defined by any of parasitemia of 5% or more, inability to take oral medicines, major organ dysfunction, severe anemia, abnormal bleeding or DIC, impaired consciousness or shock. Death can occur within hours of presentation.

This man back from Ghana without prophylaxis has ring forms on smear, 7% parasitemia and drowsiness, so he meets two severe criteria even though his blood pressure is normal. Treatment cannot wait for a repeat smear.
explain.table:
FeatureUncomplicatedSevere or complicated
SpeciesAny Plasmodium speciesUsually P. falciparum
ParasitemiaUnder 5%5% or more
Mental statusNot obtundedImpaired consciousness
Oral medicinesCan take themUnable to take them
Organs and bloodNo vital organ dysfunctionOrgan dysfunction, severe anemia, bleeding or DIC, shock
why: A normal blood pressure does not make malaria uncomplicated when parasitemia and mental status already meet severe criteria.
Severe malaria is usually falciparum, so the likely species argues for severe disease, and uncomplicated malaria can occur with any species.
Severe malaria can kill within hours, so it is recognized at presentation and treated promptly, not after a repeat smear.
Ring forms inside red cells confirm malaria, and fever in a traveler from a malarious area is malaria until proven otherwise.
explain.takeaway: Severe malaria, usually falciparum, is defined by any of parasitemia of 5% or more, impaired consciousness, inability to take oral medicines, organ dysfunction, severe anemia, bleeding or DIC, or shock, and it can kill within hours.

questions.stem:
A 19-year-old college student returns from 6 weeks in Bangladesh, where she ate at roadside stalls. Over the past 10 days her fever has climbed a little higher each day and is now 39.8 C (103.6 F). Heart rate is 78/min. She has diffuse abdominal pain and a few faint, blanching pink macules on the trunk. A malaria smear is negative.

Which test is most likely to identify the cause?
choices: Blood culture
Dengue serology
Stool ova and parasite exam
Urine histoplasma antigen
Zika PCR of urine

explain.html:
Typhoid (enteric) fever is caused by Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi, and in the US about 75% of cases are acquired during travel. Its classic course unfolds by week: in the first week a step-wise fever with bacteremia; in the second week relative bradycardia, abdominal pain and rose spots; in the third week hepatosplenomegaly, intestinal bleeding and perforation. Diagnosis is by blood culture, stool culture and bone marrow culture. Treatment is a fluoroquinolone, cephalosporin or azithromycin guided by susceptibility testing, and prevention combines immunization with caution about food and water.

This student ate at roadside stalls in Bangladesh, and over 10 days her fever has climbed a little each day to 39.8 C with a heart rate of only 78, abdominal pain and faint pink macules on the trunk, which places her in the second week of typhoid. Because the illness is bacteremic from the start, a blood culture is the test most likely to grow the organism, and her negative malaria smear has already addressed the first diagnosis to exclude.

IllnessAgent and spreadCluesDiagnosis
MalariaPlasmodium, mosquitoFever after a malarious areaSTAT smear
Typhoid feverSalmonella Typhi, food and waterStep-wise fever, relative bradycardia, rose spotsBlood, stool, bone marrow culture
DengueFlavivirus, AedesAbrupt fever, retro-orbital pain, leukopenia, warning signs at defervescenceSerology, PCR
ChikungunyaAlphavirus, AedesSevere arthralgia, persistent arthritisSerology, viral culture, PCR
ZikaFlavivirus, AedesLow-grade fever, pruritic rash, conjunctivitisPCR, serology
why: Dengue starts abruptly with retro-orbital pain, myalgia and rash, not a fever that climbs step-wise with relative bradycardia and rose spots.
An ova and parasite exam looks for parasites, while typhoid is a bacteremic Salmonella infection.
Histoplasma antigen tests for an endemic mycosis acquired by inhaling soil fungi, not an enteric fever after travel.
Zika causes a mild illness with low-grade fever, itchy rash and conjunctivitis that resolves in 2 to 7 days, not 10 days of climbing fever.
explain.takeaway: Typhoid fever presents with step-wise fever and bacteremia in week one, relative bradycardia, abdominal pain and rose spots in week two, and bleeding or perforation in week three, and blood culture is a key diagnostic test.

questions.stem:
A 30-year-old woman returns from Colombia with a low-grade fever, an itchy maculopapular rash, pain in the small joints of her hands and feet, and red eyes without discharge. Her symptoms resolve in 5 days. She hopes to become pregnant in the next year.

Which feature of the most likely infection matters most for her plans?
choices: It causes chronic inflammatory arthritis that limits fertility
It can pass to a fetus and cause congenital microcephaly
It can be prevented in a future pregnancy with a live vaccine
It predisposes to hemorrhagic shock on a second infection
It requires a course of antiviral therapy before conception

explain.html:
Zika, dengue and chikungunya are all spread by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus and overlap clinically, so comparing their features is how they are told apart. Zika is a flavivirus, and only about 20% of infected people have symptoms: low-grade fever, a pruritic maculopapular rash, arthralgia of the small joints of the hands and feet, and nonpurulent conjunctivitis, resolving in 2 to 7 days. Dengue brings more fever, myalgia, headache and hemorrhage, while chikungunya brings the most severe arthralgia and inflammatory arthritis. Zika is neurotropic, causing congenital microcephaly, Guillain-Barre syndrome, myelitis and meningoencephalitis, and it also spreads maternal-fetal, sexually, by blood products and by organ transplantation.

This woman's mild illness with itchy rash, small-joint pain and red eyes without discharge after Colombia fits Zika, and because she hopes to conceive, its passage to a fetus with congenital microcephaly matters most. There is no vaccine, and after infection the advice is to refrain from unprotected sex for at least 3 months for men and at least 8 weeks for women.
why: Chronic inflammatory arthritis with prolonged morning stiffness is the chikungunya feature, and nothing here links it to fertility.
There is no Zika vaccine; prevention is avoidance.
Hemorrhage and shock are dengue features, not Zika.
There is no antiviral therapy for Zika; planning around pregnancy centers on avoiding infection and timing unprotected sex.
explain.takeaway: Zika, an Aedes-borne flavivirus, causes low-grade fever, pruritic rash, small-joint arthralgia and nonpurulent conjunctivitis, spreads maternal-fetally and sexually, causes congenital microcephaly, and has no vaccine.
explain.subject: Microbiology

rows.why: There is no Zika vaccine; prevention is avoidance.

questions.stem:
A 55-year-old woman returns from India with abrupt high fever and severe, symmetric joint pain in her wrists, hands and ankles, with a maculopapular rash. Testing confirms a mosquito-borne virus. Four months later her fever and rash are long gone, but she still has joint pain with prolonged morning stiffness.

Which virus family caused her illness?
choices: Flavivirus, the family that also includes dengue
Picornavirus, a family that also includes hepatitis A
Flavivirus, the family that also includes yellow fever
Bunyavirus, a family spread by ticks and sandflies
Alphavirus, a different family from dengue and Zika

explain.html:
The mosquito-borne viruses that cause fever in returning travelers belong to two families: dengue, Zika and yellow fever are flaviviruses, while chikungunya is an alphavirus, spread by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus. Chikungunya was first identified in Tanzania in the 1950s and reached the Americas in December 2013, with both imported and local transmission. On the comparison of features, it has the most severe arthralgia and is the only one of the three with inflammatory arthritis marked by prolonged morning stiffness. Its hallmark is persistent arthritis or arthralgia after the acute illness, while severe complications such as respiratory failure, meningoencephalitis, hepatitis and renal failure are uncommon.

This woman back from India with abrupt high fever, severe symmetric joint pain and rash, who still has joint pain and morning stiffness four months later, has chikungunya, an alphavirus. Diagnosis is by serology, viral culture or PCR, treatment is supportive, and prevention is avoidance or one of two vaccines, a live-attenuated and a virus-like particle vaccine.

Hepatitis A spreads by the fecal-oral route and is prevented by vaccine before travel; it is not the mosquito-borne virus behind this arthritis.
Yellow fever is a flavivirus; chikungunya is not.
Chikungunya is spread by Aedes mosquitoes and is an alphavirus, not a bunyavirus.
explain.takeaway: Chikungunya is an Aedes-borne alphavirus whose hallmark is severe arthralgia followed by persistent inflammatory arthritis, while dengue, Zika and yellow fever are flaviviruses.

questions.stem:
A laboratory receives a lung biopsy from a patient with a chronic pneumonia acquired in the Ohio River valley. Cultured at room temperature (25 C), the organism grows as a fluffy mold with hyphae and large spiny spores. Grown at 37 C, the same organism grows as small oval yeasts, the form seen inside the patient's macrophages.

Which statement about this group of fungi is correct?
choices: Infection follows inhalation of the yeast form shed by infected people
Infection usually follows inhaling the mold form from the environment
They grow as molds at body temperature and as yeasts in the soil
They cause disease only in immunocompromised hosts and never reactivate later
They spread from person to person by respiratory droplets in crowds

explain.html:
The endemic mycoses share a pattern. Each lives in a specific ecologic niche in the environment and shows temperature dimorphism: it grows as a mold at 25 to 35 C in the environment and as a yeast, or spherules, at body temperature. Infection follows inhalation of the mold phase, with Sporothrix schenckii as the exception because it enters by inoculation. Severity depends on the extent of exposure and the host's immune status, hematogenous dissemination is common, and reactivation years later can occur.

This organism grew as a mold with large spiny spores at room temperature and as small oval yeasts at 37 C, the form seen inside macrophages, from a patient exposed in the Ohio River valley, which is Histoplasma capsulatum. The patient breathed in the environmental mold form, and body temperature converted it to the yeast that appears in tissue.
why: The yeast form lives in tissue, and infection comes from inhaling the environmental mold form, not from other people.
This reverses dimorphism: these fungi are molds in the environment and yeasts or spherules at body temperature.
Severity depends on exposure and immune status, so healthy people are infected too, and reactivation years later is a recognized feature.
These fungi are acquired from the environment, not passed between people by droplets.
explain.takeaway: Endemic mycoses are thermally dimorphic, molds at 25 to 35 C in the environment and yeasts or spherules at body temperature, and are acquired by inhaling the mold phase, except Sporothrix, which is inoculated.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 52-year-old man from northern Wisconsin who cuts firewood and hunts near rivers has had a cough for 6 weeks despite a course of antibiotics, and now has a raised, crusted, warty skin lesion on his forearm that slowly enlarged. A smear of material scraped from the lesion is examined.

What is the smear most likely to show?
choices: Small oval yeasts packed inside macrophages
Cigar-shaped yeasts with no hyphae in the lesion
Large spherules filled with many small endospores
Large thick-walled yeasts with one broad-based bud
Rope-like hyphae branching at right angles

explain.html:
Each endemic mycosis has its own niche, map and tissue form, which is how they are told apart. Blastomyces dermatitidis lives in soil and decaying wood, and its endemic area spans the Great Lakes, the Mississippi and Ohio River valleys and the Southeast. Like the others it is inhaled in the mold phase and converts to a yeast at body temperature, and disease is pulmonary or extrapulmonary, so a skin lesion after a lung illness represents spread beyond the lung. In tissue it appears as a large, thick-walled yeast with a single broad-based bud. Diagnosis is by fungal smear and culture with a DNA probe and by antigen detection, more sensitive in urine than serum, and treatment is amphotericin or itraconazole.

This Wisconsin woodcutter has a 6-week cough that did not respond to antibiotics and a slowly enlarging warty skin lesion, so a scraping should show the broad-based budding yeast of blastomycosis.
explain.table:
FungusNiche and regionRouteTissue formTreatment
Histoplasma capsulatumNitrogen-rich soil (guano); Ohio and Mississippi valleysInhaled moldSmall yeasts inside macrophagesAmphotericin, itraconazole
Blastomyces dermatitidisSoil and decaying wood; Great Lakes, Ohio and Mississippi valleys, SoutheastInhaled moldLarge thick-walled yeast, broad-based budAmphotericin, itraconazole
Coccidioides immitis and posadasiiCalifornia and the desert SouthwestInhaled moldSpherules filled with endosporesAmphotericin, fluconazole
Sporothrix schenckiiSoil, moss, hay, decaying vegetationInoculation into skinCigar-shaped yeastsItraconazole, amphotericin

Cigar-shaped yeasts are the tissue form of Sporothrix, which enters the skin by inoculation without a preceding cough.
Spherules filled with endospores are the tissue form of Coccidioides, from the desert Southwest.
Hyphae belong to the mold phase grown in the environment or at room temperature, not the yeast seen in tissue at body temperature.
explain.takeaway: Blastomyces dermatitidis, from soil and decaying wood around the Great Lakes and the Ohio and Mississippi valleys, spreads from lung to skin and appears in tissue as large thick-walled yeasts with broad-based buds.

questions.stem:
A 34-year-old construction worker who moved from New Jersey to Bakersfield, California, digs foundations in dry, dusty soil. After a windstorm he develops fever, cough and pleuritic chest pain. A lung biopsy is obtained after symptoms persist.

Which finding in the biopsy and which oral drug fit this infection?
choices: Small intracellular yeasts; treat with nafcillin
Gram-negative coccobacilli; treat with doxycycline
Broad-based budding yeasts; treat with metronidazole
Cigar-shaped yeasts; treat with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
Spherules filled with endospores; treat with fluconazole

explain.html:
Coccidioides is the endemic mycosis of the southwestern deserts: C. immitis in California and C. posadasii outside California. Like the other dimorphic fungi, it is inhaled from soil in the mold phase, but at body temperature it forms spherules filled with endospores rather than a budding yeast. Disease can be pulmonary or extrapulmonary. Diagnosis is by fungal smear and culture, serology, histopathology and PCR. Treatment is amphotericin and fluconazole, with itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole and isavuconazole as alternatives.

This construction worker digging dry soil in Bakersfield developed fever, cough and pleuritic pain after a windstorm, and his biopsy should show endospore-filled spherules. Fluconazole is the azole listed with amphotericin as treatment for this mycosis.
why: Small intracellular yeasts describe Histoplasma, and nafcillin is an antibacterial, not an antifungal.
No bacterial cause fits a fungal biopsy after desert dust exposure.
Broad-based budding yeasts describe Blastomyces, and metronidazole is not an antifungal.
Cigar-shaped yeasts describe Sporothrix, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is not among its treatments.
explain.takeaway: Coccidioides (immitis in California, posadasii elsewhere in the Southwest) is inhaled from desert soil, forms endospore-filled spherules in tissue, and is treated with fluconazole or amphotericin.

questions.stem:
A 61-year-old avid gardener who works with sphagnum moss and hay pricks her finger. Three weeks later a painless nodule forms at the site and ulcerates, and a second nodule appears higher on the same forearm. She has no cough or fever. Culture of the lesion at room temperature grows a mold with delicate flower-like clusters of spores.

How did she most likely acquire this infection, and what is the treatment?
choices: Inhalation of spores from soil; amphotericin is required for all cases
Mosquito bite; supportive care because no therapy exists
Inhalation of bird droppings; urine antigen guides fluconazole
Inoculation through the skin; itraconazole is a treatment of choice
Ingestion of contaminated produce; azithromycin is preferred

explain.html:
Most endemic mycoses are acquired by inhaling the mold phase, but Sporothrix schenckii is the exception: it is primarily a cutaneous disease following inoculation. It lives in soil, moss, hay and decaying vegetation, so a puncture while gardening or handling hay introduces it into the skin. Its lesions stay in the skin rather than starting in the lung, which is why there is no cough or fever. Diagnosis is by fungal smear and culture; at room temperature it grows as a mold with flower-like clusters of spores, and in tissue it appears as cigar-shaped yeasts. Treatment is itraconazole, with amphotericin as the alternative.

This gardener who works with sphagnum moss and hay pricked her finger, and three weeks later she has an ulcerating nodule with a second one higher on the forearm and no lung symptoms, which is sporotrichosis acquired through the skin.
why: Sporothrix is the endemic mycosis acquired by inoculation, not inhalation, and itraconazole is a treatment of choice.
Mosquito-borne infections with only supportive care are dengue, chikungunya and Zika, not a fungal skin nodule.
Bird and bat droppings and a urine antigen point to histoplasmosis, and fluconazole is not its listed treatment.
Ingestion and azithromycin fit febrile travelers' diarrhea, not a fungal skin infection.
explain.takeaway: Sporothrix schenckii is inoculated into the skin from soil, moss or hay, unlike the inhaled endemic mycoses, causing cutaneous nodules that are treated with itraconazole.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 67-year-old man who had his thymus removed for a thymoma 6 years ago is traveling to the Amazon basin of Brazil, an area that requires protection against a mosquito-borne flavivirus that causes hemorrhagic fever and has no antiviral treatment. He has never received the live-attenuated vaccine for it.

Which serious vaccine complication is he at increased risk for, and how does it present?
choices: Guillain-Barre syndrome from direct viral invasion of peripheral nerves
Anaphylaxis that becomes more likely with each booster dose given
Congenital microcephaly in any child conceived within 3 months after the dose
Chronic inflammatory arthritis lasting months after the vaccine
A multisystem illness like natural disease, days after a first dose

explain.html:
Yellow fever is a flavivirus carried by mosquitoes (Aedes aegypti, Haemagogus and Sabethes) that ranges from a self-limited flu-like illness to hemorrhagic fever with a high case-fatality rate, and it has no anti-infective therapy. A live-attenuated vaccine gives lifelong protection after a single dose. Its caveats come in three kinds: uncommon immediate hypersensitivity, vaccine-associated neurologic disease (YEL-AND), and vaccine-associated viscerotropic disease (YEL-AVD). YEL-AVD mimics natural yellow fever, starts a median of 3 days after vaccination, is fatal in 65% of cases, and has occurred only after a first vaccination, never a booster. Its risk factors are older age and thymus disease or thymectomy.

This 67-year-old who lost his thymus to a thymoma and is about to receive his first yellow fever vaccine carries both risk factors, so the complication to weigh is a multisystem illness resembling yellow fever days after the dose.
explain.table:
FeatureYEL-AND (neurologic)YEL-AVD (viscerotropic)
PictureMeningoencephalitis (direct CNS invasion); Guillain-Barre syndrome, ADEM, bulbar palsy (autoimmune)Mimics natural yellow fever
OutcomeSerious but rarely fatalDeath in 65%
Key factsSeveral distinct syndromesMedian onset 3 days; first dose only; risk with older age, thymus disease or thymectomy
why: Guillain-Barre syndrome after the vaccine is a form of YEL-AND that is autoimmune, not direct viral invasion, and his risk factors point to viscerotropic disease.
Immediate hypersensitivity is uncommon and is not tied to boosters, and his risk factors match YEL-AVD instead.
Congenital microcephaly is a complication of Zika infection, not of the yellow fever vaccine.
Persistent arthritis or arthralgia after the acute illness is the hallmark of chikungunya, not a yellow fever vaccine effect.
explain.takeaway: Yellow fever vaccine-associated viscerotropic disease mimics yellow fever about 3 days after a first dose, is fatal in about 65%, and is more likely with older age and thymus disease or thymectomy.

questions.stem:
A 31-year-old man backpacking in Southeast Asia develops fever of 38.9 C (102 F), severe abdominal cramps and frequent small stools with visible blood. He is confined to his room and cannot continue traveling. He is drinking oral rehydration solution and asks which antibiotic he should take.

Which choice is preferred for his illness?
choices: Rifaximin
Loperamide alone
Azithromycin
Bismuth subsalicylate alone
No antibiotic, only fluids

explain.html:
Treatment of travelers' diarrhea follows severity, and fluid replacement comes first for everyone. Mild diarrhea, which does not interfere with activities, can be managed with bismuth or an antimotility agent (loperamide or diphenoxylate) to reduce stooling. Moderate diarrhea is distressing or interferes with activities, and severe diarrhea is incapacitating or includes dysentery with bloody stools; both are treated with an antibiotic. Azithromycin is preferred for dysentery or febrile diarrhea, while rifaximin and rifamycin should not be used in those settings, and fluoroquinolones carry adverse effects and resistance concerns.

This backpacker has a fever of 38.9 C, severe cramps and bloody stools and is confined to his room, which makes it severe, febrile, dysenteric diarrhea. He keeps drinking oral rehydration solution and adds azithromycin.

SeverityDefinitionTreatment

MildDoes not interfere with activitiesBismuth or antimotility agent (loperamide, diphenoxylate)
ModerateDistressing or interferes with activitiesAntibiotic
SevereIncapacitating, dysentery or bloody stoolsAntibiotic: azithromycin preferred for dysentery or fever; not rifaximin or rifamycin
why: Rifaximin is not for dysentery or febrile diarrhea, and he has both.
An antimotility agent alone fits mild diarrhea that does not interfere with activities, not febrile dysentery.
Bismuth alone is for mild diarrhea that does not interfere with activities.
Fluids are essential, but severe, febrile, bloody diarrhea also warrants an antibiotic.
explain.takeaway: Travelers' diarrhea is treated by severity: fluids for all, bismuth or antimotility agents for mild disease, and azithromycin for dysentery or febrile diarrhea, where rifaximin is avoided.

questions.stem:
A 27-year-old man returned from Puerto Rico 5 days ago. He had abrupt fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, myalgias and a rash. Today his fever has broken, and he feels he is getting better, but he now has persistent vomiting, abdominal tenderness and bleeding gums.

[[labs 0]]

Which statement best describes his current situation?
choices: He is in the convalescent phase and can be discharged with oral fluids
He is in the critical phase, with warning signs of plasma leakage
He needs an antiviral drug started now to prevent severe dengue
He has developed a bacterial superinfection that broke his fever
He has typhoid, since fever that resolves then recurs is step-wise

explain.html:
Dengue is caused by one of four dengue viruses of the genus Flavivirus, spread by Aedes aegypti or Aedes albopictus, and ranges from asymptomatic infection to severe disease. After a 5 to 7 day incubation it begins abruptly and moves through three phases. The febrile phase lasts 2 to 7 days with headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia, rash and minor bleeding. The critical phase begins at defervescence and lasts 24 to 48 hours; most patients improve, but those with significant plasma leakage can progress to severe dengue before the convalescent phase. Warning signs that predict progression are abdominal pain or tenderness, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, hepatomegaly and edema.

This man's fever broke today, and he now has persistent vomiting, abdominal tenderness and bleeding gums, with leukopenia, low platelets and a rising hematocrit, so he is in the critical phase with warning signs and needs close monitoring rather than discharge. Treatment is supportive, since there is no antiviral therapy.
explain.table:
PhaseTimingWhat happens
FebrileFever 2 to 7 days, can be biphasicHeadache, retro-orbital pain, arthralgia or myalgia, rash, minor bleeding; warning signs can appear late
CriticalBegins at defervescence, lasts 24 to 48 hoursMost improve; significant plasma leakage can progress to severe dengue
ConvalescentAfter the critical phaseRecovery
why: Defervescence begins the critical phase, not convalescence, and his warning signs demand close monitoring.
There is no antiviral therapy for dengue; treatment is supportive.
The fever broke as part of the natural move into the critical phase, not because of a bacterial superinfection.
Typhoid fever climbs step-wise over a week with relative bradycardia; it does not start abruptly with retro-orbital pain and then break.
explain.takeaway: Dengue's critical phase begins at defervescence and lasts 24 to 48 hours, and warning signs such as abdominal pain, persistent vomiting and mucosal bleeding signal plasma leakage and possible severe dengue; care is supportive.

questions.stem:
A 46-year-old man from Kentucky spent a weekend clearing out an old barn where bats and pigeons roosted. Two weeks later he has fever, dry cough and fatigue. Chest imaging shows patchy infiltrates with enlarged hilar nodes. A bronchoscopic biopsy shows macrophages packed with small oval yeasts.

Which noninvasive test is most useful to support this diagnosis?
choices: Urine or serum antigen assay
Serum coccidioidal antibody
Malaria thick and thin smear
Darkfield microscopy of sputum
Stool culture for enteric pathogens

explain.html:
Histoplasma capsulatum reaches a high concentration of its mold phase in soil rich in nitrogen, such as guano from birds and bats, and it is most highly endemic in the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys. Disturbing that soil puts the mold phase into the air, where it is inhaled and converts to small yeasts at body temperature, seen inside macrophages in tissue. Clinical disease is pulmonary or disseminated. Diagnosis uses fungal culture, an antigen assay in serum or urine, and cytology or histopathology. Treatment is amphotericin or itraconazole, with voriconazole, posaconazole or isavuconazole as alternatives.

This Kentucky man who cleared a barn full of bats and pigeons has pneumonia with hilar nodes two weeks later and macrophages packed with small yeasts on biopsy, so histoplasmosis is the diagnosis, and the antigen assay is the noninvasive test that supports it while cultures grow.
why: Coccidioidal serology tests for the mycosis of California and the desert Southwest, not an Ohio valley guano exposure.
A malaria smear is for fever in a traveler from a malarious area, not a fungal pneumonia after barn cleaning.
Darkfield microscopy is not among the tests for histoplasmosis, which are culture, antigen assay and histopathology.
Stool culture looks for enteric bacteria, not a fungus causing pneumonia.
explain.takeaway: Histoplasma capsulatum concentrates in bird and bat guano in the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys, appears as small yeasts inside macrophages, and is supported noninvasively by a serum or urine antigen assay.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 34-year-old man returned 12 days ago from 3 weeks in Ghana. He took doxycycline during the trip but stopped it on the flight home. He has had 4 days of fever and chills, and today he is drowsy, confused about the date, and has vomited every pill and sip of fluid since morning. Temperature is 39.8 C (103.6 F), pulse 112/min, and blood pressure 108/70 mm Hg. A thin smear shows Plasmodium falciparum ring forms with 1.5% parasitemia. Hemoglobin is 11.8 g/dL (normal 13.5 to 17.5), and platelets are 95,000/mm3 (normal 150,000 to 400,000).

Which statement best describes his malaria and the reason?
choices: Uncomplicated, since partial prophylaxis keeps the malaria mild
Severe, but only because the species on his smear is falciparum
Severe, since confusion defines it at any level of parasitemia
Uncomplicated until a repeat smear shows that parasitemia is rising
Uncomplicated, since his parasitemia is still below the 5% cutoff

explain.html:
Fever in a traveler returning from a malarious area is malaria until proven otherwise, and the next decision is whether the illness is uncomplicated or severe. Uncomplicated malaria can occur with any Plasmodium species and requires all of the following: parasitemia below 5%, not obtunded, able to take oral medicines, and no evidence of vital organ dysfunction. Severe malaria, usually falciparum, is present when any one criterion is met: parasitemia of 5% or more, inability to take oral medications, organ dysfunction, severe anemia, abnormal bleeding or DIC, impaired consciousness, or shock. Death can occur within hours of presentation.

This man's parasitemia of 1.5% is below the cutoff, but he is confused and cannot keep any pill down, and each of those alone defines severe disease. The low parasitemia is the trap. He also stopped doxycycline on the flight home instead of continuing it for 4 weeks after leaving the endemic area, which explains how he became infected.
explain.table:
Uncomplicated (needs all)Severe (needs any one)
Parasitemia below 5%Parasitemia 5% or more
Not obtundedImpaired consciousness
Can take oral medicinesUnable to take oral medications
No vital organ dysfunctionOrgan dysfunction, severe anemia, bleeding or DIC, shock
why: Doxycycline must continue 4 weeks after leaving the endemic area; stopping early is how he got infected, not a reason for mild disease.
Falciparum causes most severe disease, but uncomplicated falciparum malaria exists; severity comes from the criteria.
He already meets severe criteria now, and severe malaria can kill within hours, so there is no waiting for a repeat smear.
Parasitemia below 5% is necessary but not sufficient; he is obtunded and cannot take oral drugs.
explain.takeaway: Malaria is uncomplicated only if every condition is met (parasitemia below 5%, alert, taking oral drugs, no organ dysfunction); any single severe criterion, such as impaired consciousness, makes it severe.
explain.topic: Severe malaria is defined by any one criterion
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 44-year-old man from Phoenix, Arizona, is hospitalized in New Jersey with 3 weeks of fever, cough, and pleuritic chest pain. A lung biopsy shows spherules filled with endospores, and part of the specimen is sent for fungal culture. He coughs frequently, and several nurses care for him closely for 10 days before the diagnosis is made; none becomes ill. The culture plate is mistakenly left on a bench at room temperature instead of in the 37 C incubator, and after 10 days a microbiology technologist opens it on the open bench to examine the growth. Two weeks afterward the technologist develops fever, cough, and a lung infiltrate.

Which best explains why the technologist became infected but the nurses did not?
choices: The technologist had reactivation of an old, silent infection
His cough spread spherules only to people at very close range
The plate grew yeasts, which are more infectious than spherules
The plate held the inhaled mold form; his tissue held spherules
The nurses were protected once he began taking fluconazole

explain.html:
The endemic mycoses each occupy a specific ecologic niche in the environment and share temperature dimorphism: they grow as mold in the environment at 25 to 35 C and as yeasts, or spherules, at body temperature. Infection follows inhalation of the organism in the mold phase (Sporothrix, acquired by inoculation, is the exception), and the severity of infection depends on the extent of exposure and immune status. Hematogenous dissemination and reactivation years later are both common.

Coccidioides lives in the soil of the desert southwest, and in tissue it forms spherules filled with endospores, as in this patient's biopsy. That tissue form is not the infectious form, so his cough posed no risk to the nurses. The culture plate incubated at room temperature grew the mold form, and opening it on an open bench delivered a large inhaled dose to the technologist, who became ill 2 weeks later.

SettingTemperatureFormInfectious by inhalation?
Environment or culture at room temperature25 to 35 CMoldYes

why: Reactivation happens years after an earlier infection, and this illness followed a clear new exposure by 2 weeks.
The tissue form, spherules, is not the infectious form, and the endemic mycoses are acquired by inhaling mold, not from coughing patients.
At room temperature the fungus grows as mold; yeasts and spherules are the body-temperature forms.
The nurses' exposure happened before any diagnosis or antifungal treatment.
explain.takeaway: Endemic dimorphic fungi grow as mold at 25 to 35 C and as yeasts or spherules at 37 C; inhaled mold, not the tissue form in a patient, causes infection.
explain.topic: Thermal dimorphism decides who gets infected
